key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: SUDDEN onset during trauma - fall, direct blow, or high-energy impact. Common in elderly with osteoporosis. LOCATION: Femoral neck, intertrochanteric, or subtrochanteric region. DURATION: Immediate severe pain that persists. CHARACTER: SEVERE, SHARP, CONSTANT pain. AGGRAVATING: ANY weight bearing, hip movement, leg movement. RELIEVING: NOTHING relieves pain until immobilization. Patient cannot bear weight. TIMING: Immediate severe pain that persists until surgical fixation. SEVERITY: 8-10/10, severe and unrelenting. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: UNABLE TO BEAR WEIGHT, leg appears shortened and externally rotated, severe pain with any movement, may have audible 'snap' or 'crack' at injury. KEY POSITIVES: Bony tenderness over hip, deformity, inability to bear weight, positive log roll test, positive heel strike test. KEY NEGATIVES: No open wound (rules out open fracture), no crepitus unless severe.

includes.patient_friendly: all at once or very quickly

red_flags: Open wound with bone visible - open fracture, call 911
Severe pain with neurovascular compromise - cold, pale, pulseless leg, call 911
Elderly patients with minimal trauma - possible pathological fracture, needs urgent evaluation
High-energy trauma - possible associated injuries, needs urgent evaluation
Severe pain with inability to move leg - possible nerve injury or compartment syndrome
